description: I am a computer engineering student with the hope of solving problems for the world to be a happy space.
summary:
Lunar Odyssey is a free browser game where students run a crewed outpost at Shackleton crater, near the Moon’s south pole, where NASA’s Artemis astronauts are headed. Every day brings real trade-offs:

Power: solar panels or the fission reactor.
Life support: oxygen and water, kept running while ice is mined from permanently shadowed craters.
Food: packed meals, a lettuce greenhouse and cargo landers.
Radiation shielding: get the crew into the storm shelter in time, or keep working.

Drive the rover yourself or send astronauts out on foot, but every kilometre costs battery, air and time.

The numbers come from NASA, including live solar flares from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database, LRO terrain and lighting, and Apollo moonquake records. Hazards play out the way they really would, in short scenes where the crew explain what is happening. In return, every choice has real consequences: a skipped shelter means real radiation dose, and a dead battery strands the rover.

Cadet and Specialist modes let younger and older learners play the same mission at the right level. Lunar Odyssey makes the mission’s engineering trade-offs real enough to learn from and fun enough to keep playing. Play at gravity-benders-mockups.vercel.app.

Everything it mentions is in the game: the greenhouse, the fission reactor and solar power, the storm shelter, the Cadet and Specialist modes, and manual driving.
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Odyssey puts students in command of a crewed outpost at Shackleton crater, at the Moon’s south pole. Each game day you choose how to spend limited work hours, power and supplies, then live with the results:

Power: Solar panels need sunlight on the crater rim, a fission reactor gives steady power, and a solar mast can be built. Batteries run down in the dark.

Life support: Oxygen is made by splitting recycled water, as on the ISS. Water must be mined as ice from permanently shadowed craters and carried home by the rover.

Food: Packed meals run down, a greenhouse grows lettuce in about 28 days (as in NASA’s Veggie experiment), and a cargo lander brings supplies mid-mission.

Radiation shielding: Solar flares and storms arrive with real-world timing. Do you shelter the crew and lose work hours, or keep going and take the dose? Doses are tracked in mSv against NASA’s 30-day limit.

Exploration: Players drive the MO-01 rover themselves or let it drive automatically, or send an astronaut out on foot in Moon gravity. Every kilometre costs battery, air and time, and a 2 km walk-back rule keeps astronauts close enough to walk home.

Hazards (flares, meteorite strikes, moonquakes, invisible solar storms, crew illness) play out in short 3D scenes. A voiced crew and Mission Control explain what is happening and why. Choices have consequences: a skipped shelter raises the dose, and Kofi gets radiation sickness. A dead battery strands the rover, and an empty water tank stops oxygen production.

Benefits and intended impact

The game makes the trade-offs that decide a mission’s success something you can see and feel, without hiding them or burying players in jargon. Cadet mode (ages 7–12) and Specialist mode (13+) give the same mission at two depths. It runs free in any browser, on phones and laptops, with no install or account, so a classroom can start in seconds. A 3-minute guided tour for judges and teachers and a 30-second self-playing demo make it easy to show. Our aim is for students to finish knowing why the south pole matters, why water ice is precious, and that every choice on a real mission costs something else.

Real NASA data

Live: solar flares and energetic particle events from NASA’s DONKI space-weather database (last 30 days) set how stormy the Sun is in each game.

Saved: 65,536 LRO LOLA laser heights of Shackleton crater build the 3D Moon, the minimap and the mission map.

Saved: NASA life-support values for oxygen per person per day, ISS water recycling, the NASA-STD-3001 radiation limit, Artemis spacesuit limits and the Veggie growth time.

Saved: crew blood data from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (Inspiration4), used for how colds spread on the base.

Saved: LRO images of fresh craters and Apollo seismometer findings.

An in-game “Where the data comes from” panel lists every source, and a “What we simplified” section says honestly where we changed things.

Tools and technologies

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page

Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D lunar surface, the base, the rover, astronauts and the film-style scenes

SVG for the base and mission maps

Web Speech API for the voiced crew, with captions that follow the voice

Web Audio API for sound effects such as the dosimeter clicks

NASA DONKI API, LRO LOLA, OSDR and other NASA datasets

GitHub for version control and Vercel for hosting

Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant

AI-generated concept art, clearly labelled in the game as not NASA data

What makes it creative

Hazards follow real physics, not movie physics. A meteorite strikes with no warning and no shooting star; the dust flies in clean arcs with no cloud. A moonquake is silent but rings for minutes, so the crew feel it rather than hear it. A solar storm on the Moon is invisible: no clouds or blowing dust, just specks on the camera and a clicking dosimeter. A flare’s light arrives minutes before its particles.

The data is live, so no two games have quite the same Sun.

Players can feel radiation: an astronaut out in a flare sees flashes of light, as Apollo astronauts did, and a sick astronaut staggers and doubles over.

Factors we considered

Accuracy vs. fun: distances are shrunk and the clock runs faster, but walking and driving still cost the real time, air and battery. We tell players what we simplified.

Age range: two difficulty modes, short sentences, voiced lines with captions, and Mission Control explanations at each decision.

Access: free, browser-based and phone-friendly, with a lighter mode for older phones, touch controls, keyboard controls and reduced-motion support.

Honesty: sources are named in the game, and imagined parts (the crew, the base layout, the MO-01 rover and the concept art) are labelled as imagined.
